name: St Bavo’s Cathedral
blurb: Built from the 13th to the 16th century, with an 89 m tower. Inside hangs the Van Eyck brothers’ Adoration of the Mystic Lamb (1432), one of the most famous and most stolen paintings in the world. Its Just Judges panel, stolen in 1934, has never been found.
text: St Bavo’s Cathedral is the cathedral of the diocese of Ghent and one of the great Gothic churches of the Low Countries. From outside you mostly see its heavy 89 m west tower, which rises above the roofs of the old town and, with the Belfry and St Nicholas’ Church, forms Ghent’s famous row of three towers. Step inside and you can see how the church grew over three centuries: a lofty Gothic choir, a lighter late-Gothic nave and, underneath, a crypt from Romanesque times.

Its treasure is the Ghent Altarpiece, the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, which Hubert and Jan van Eyck finished in 1432. On its twelve panels you see Adam and Eve, singing angels, God enthroned and, in the middle, the Lamb on the altar, worshipped by saints, prophets, knights and pilgrims from every corner of the world. The painters used oil paint with a precision never seen before: you can make out single hairs, jewels catching the light and more than forty kinds of plant you can still recognise today.

But the cathedral is more than that one painting. There is Rubens’ St Bavo Entering the Monastery (1624), a lavish rococo pulpit by Laurent Delvaux in oak and white and black marble, Baroque bishops’ tombs and one of the largest crypts in Belgium, with wall paintings and church treasures. There is so much that you can easily spend a couple of hours.
history: A small church dedicated to St John the Baptist stood here as early as the 10th century. In the 12th century it was replaced by a Romanesque church, whose crypt survives. From the 13th century on, a new Gothic church was built bit by bit: first the choir, then in the 15th and 16th centuries the tower and the nave. That is why one building shows three centuries of architecture.

In 1432 the altarpiece was installed in the chapel of Joos Vijd and his wife Elisabeth Borluut, who had commissioned it. In 1500 the Emperor Charles V, born in Ghent, was baptised here. After the Ghent revolt of 1539 he had the old St Bavo’s Abbey torn down to build a fortress to keep the city in check; the monks moved to St John’s, which therefore became St Bavo’s. When the diocese of Ghent was founded in 1559, it became a cathedral.

The altarpiece has led an adventurous life. During the iconoclastic fury of 1566 it was hidden in the tower. French revolutionaries took the central panels to the Louvre; they came back after Napoleon’s fall. The side wings were sold in 1816 and ended up in Berlin, until after the First World War they had to be returned to Ghent. In 1934 two panels were stolen. The one with John the Baptist came back, but the Just Judges has never been found: what you see now is a copy by Jef Van der Veken. In the Second World War the Nazis seized the altarpiece; the American ‘Monuments Men’ found it in 1945 in a salt mine in Austria.

Since 2012 the altarpiece has been restored panel by panel by the Royal Institute for Cultural Heritage. Under later overpainting the Van Eycks’ original paint came to light again, the best-known surprise being the startlingly human face of the Lamb. In 2021 a new visitor centre opened in the cathedral, where you can also experience the painting’s story in augmented reality.

visit: The cathedral stands on Sint-Baafsplein, a few minutes’ walk from the Belfry and the Korenmarkt. You can usually walk into the church itself for free, outside services. For the Ghent Altarpiece you buy a ticket: it includes a tour with a tablet or AR glasses through the painting’s story, after which you stand face to face with the original. Allow an hour to an hour and a half, and in high season it is best to book ahead.
It is a place of worship: keep your voice down, cover your shoulders if asked and don’t wander about during mass. Photos without flash are allowed in most places, but not everywhere.

name: Belfry
blurb: The town’s 91 m tower, begun in 1313. Ghent kept its charters of rights here, and watchmen looked out for fire and enemies. A gilded dragon keeps watch on top. With the Cloth Hall beside it, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
text: The Belfry is the middle one of Ghent’s three towers and, at 91 m, the tallest belfry in Belgium. While the church towers either side speak of God, the Belfry stands for the city itself: for the freedom and the power of its citizens against the count. At the top of the spire turns a gilded dragon, the symbol of Ghent, keeping watch over the city with its head into the wind.

Inside, you climb past the watchmen’s rooms and the halls where the city archive was once kept to the bell floor. There hangs the carillon, one of the largest in the country with over fifty bells, and you can see the huge drum that plays them automatically. From the gallery you get one of the best views over the city: St Bavo’s right next door, the Gravensteen, the Leie with the Graslei and, on a clear day, far beyond Ghent. A lift takes you most of the way up.

Against the tower stands the Cloth Hall, where the cloth merchants had the quality of their woollen cloth inspected: the source of Ghent’s medieval wealth. On the Goudenleeuwplein side is the Mammelokker, the old entrance to the town jail. The sculpture above it shows an old man in his cell being breastfed by his daughter, a story of mercy from Roman antiquity. On the little square beside it stands the cracked bell Triomfante.
history: Building began in 1313, when Ghent was, after Paris, one of the largest cities in northern Europe. The builders worked from a design on parchment that still exists and is among the oldest architectural drawings of the Low Countries. By around 1380 the stone tower was standing, with a wooden spire on top. In the ‘secreet’, a strongroom behind thick iron doors, the city kept its privileges: the charters with the rights it had wrested from the counts.

The great bell Roland rang for fire, for war and to call the citizens together. People in Ghent still know the rhyme ‘My name is Roland; when I toll there is fire, when I ring there is a storm in Flanders.’ After the revolt of 1539 the Emperor Charles V punished the city: its privileges were revoked and Roland had to come down. The Hemony bell Triomfante, which later hung in the tower, cracked in 1914 and now stands at the foot of the Belfry.

The Cloth Hall was built against the tower from 1425, but was never quite finished until the early 20th century. The spire too went through many versions: a wooden one, a Baroque one, a cast-iron one from the 19th century and finally today’s, built for the 1913 World’s Fair after the original medieval design. The oldest dragons, from the 14th century, are kept inside the tower.

In 1999 the Belfry, with the Cloth Hall and the Mammelokker, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List, among the belfries of Belgium and France. Together these towers tell the story of the free medieval towns, where citizens ran their own city.

visit: The entrance is on the Sint-Baafsplein side, between the cathedral and the town hall. You buy a ticket and go up on foot or by lift; the last stairs to the bells and the gallery are narrow and steep. Come on a clear day for the view if you can, and check whether there is a carillon concert that day: then you hear the bells up close.
Allow about an hour. The lift is a big help if you are not steady on your feet, but not every part of the tower can be reached without stairs.

name: Gravensteen
blurb: The castle of the Counts of Flanders, built in 1180 by Philip of Alsace. It later served as a court, a prison and even a cotton mill, and got its battlements back around 1900. In 1949 students occupied it, in protest against the price of beer going up.
text: The Gravensteen is the only medieval castle in Flanders with an almost completely preserved defensive system, and it stands right in the middle of the city. A moat fed by the Leie and the Lieve surrounds a high curtain wall with turrets and battlements. You enter through the gatehouse onto the courtyard, with the keep in the middle: the count’s massive residential tower, almost thirty metres high.

Inside you wander through the count’s halls, the old cellars, the dungeons and the armoury, with suits of armour, swords and crossbows. There is also a collection of instruments of torture and punishment from the days when the castle was a court and a prison: not the place for small children who scare easily. The high point is literally the roof of the keep: from the battlements you look out over the roofs of the Patershol, the Vrijdagmarkt and the towers of the old town.

The visit comes with an audio guide in the form of an ‘audio film’: Ghent comedian Wouter Deprez tells the castle’s history with plenty of humour, and it works for young and old. So you hear about counts, rebellious Ghent folk and students on the roof as you walk through the halls.
history: There was a fortified place here as early as the 10th century, at first of wood. In 1180 Count Philip of Alsace had the stone castle built that you see today; an inscription above the gate gives the year. Philip had been on crusade and had seen the crusader castles there. His castle was also a message to the rich, rebellious people of Ghent: the count was in charge here.

After the 14th century the counts no longer lived there: they moved to the more comfortable Prinsenhof, where Charles V would be born in 1500. The Gravensteen became the seat of the Council of Flanders, the county’s highest court. Justice was done here, coins were minted, prisoners were locked up and tortured. When the Council left in the 18th century, the castle was sold and split up: houses and workshops moved in and, in the early 19th century, even a cotton mill, with workers’ houses in the courtyard.

By the end of the 19th century the Gravensteen was a crumbling ruin hidden behind houses. The city bought it and had it restored. Around 1900 it was cleared and got its walls, towers and battlements back, partly as the restorers thought a medieval castle ought to look. Just in time for the 1913 World’s Fair it stood there again like a fairy-tale castle.

In November 1949 Ghent students occupied the castle for a few hours, in protest against the price of beer. They barricaded themselves behind the battlements and pelted the police and firemen with rotten vegetables. The story became a legend, and the students still commemorate the occupation every year.

visit: The Gravensteen is on Sint-Veerleplein, five minutes’ walk from the Korenmarkt and the Graslei, on the edge of the Patershol. Buy a ticket at the desk or online in advance; the audio guide is included. Allow an hour and a half. There are many narrow spiral staircases, so the castle is only partly accessible by wheelchair or pushchair.

In summer, go early in the day or late in the afternoon: the battlements are less crowded then. Afterwards you can walk straight into the Patershol, the old quarter of narrow lanes and many restaurants.

name: Graslei and Korenlei
blurb: Ghent’s medieval port, on both banks of the Leie. Boatmen unloaded grain here and the guilds built their houses along the quay. The Koornstapelhuis, the grey Romanesque grain store from around 1200, is one of the oldest houses in town.
text: The Graslei and the Korenlei are the two quays either side of the Leie, in the heart of Ghent, and together the city’s best-known postcard view. On the Graslei, the east side, stands a row of guild houses and warehouses showing almost a thousand years of architecture: from a plain Romanesque granary to ornate Baroque façades. Across the water, on the Korenlei, stand stately mansions and more guild houses. In between lie the little boats, and the Leie drifts slowly towards the centre.

Walk along the Graslei and read the façades like a book. The Guild House of the Free Boatmen is late Gothic, with a ship as its weathervane. The narrow Toll House, where toll was levied on grain, is Flemish Renaissance. The Koornstapelhuis, the grey Romanesque granary with the stepped gable, is one of the oldest houses in town. And the Grain Measurers’ House was for the men who weighed and measured the grain. On the Korenlei, the Guild House of the Unfree Boatmen stands out, with its Baroque front and gilded ship.

Today this is Ghent’s living room. On sunny days hundreds of people sit on the quay wall with their legs above the water, there are café terraces, and the canal boats leave from here. In the evening the façades are softly lit: Ghent has its own lighting plan, and the Graslei is its finest example. The best view of both quays is from St Michael’s Bridge.
history: This stretch of the Leie was Ghent’s medieval port, called ‘Tussen Bruggen’ (Between Bridges). Ghent held the staple right for grain: ships carrying grain on the Leie and the Scheldt first had to offer it for sale here. That right made the city rich and kept its people fed. Boatmen unloaded their cargo, grain measurers checked the measures and the grain was stored in warehouses.

The guilds, the associations of craftsmen and traders, showed off their wealth with splendid houses on the quay. The Koornstapelhuis was built around 1200 as a grain store. The Guild House of the Free Boatmen followed in 1531, the Toll House in 1682 and the Grain Measurers’ House at the end of the 17th century. The free boatmen could sail anywhere; the unfree boatmen only within the city, and they built their own guild house on the Korenlei in 1739.

In the 19th century the port lost its importance and many façades were altered or hidden behind plaster. For the 1913 World’s Fair the Graslei was thoroughly restored, so that visitors could see a medieval Ghent. Some façades were rebuilt from old drawings in the process. The Masons’ Guild House on the Graslei is one such reconstruction: later the real façade turned out to still exist, hidden in a lane by St Nicholas’ Church, where it has since been restored too.

For a long time cars drove along the Graslei and the Korenlei. Since the centre became largely car-free the quays belong to people on foot again, and they have become the place where Ghent comes together, from summer evenings with friends to the Ghent Festival.
dates: The Koornstapelhuis, a Romanesque granary.

visit: The Graslei and the Korenlei are always open to everyone, day and night. They are a few minutes’ walk from the Korenmarkt or St Michael’s Bridge. The guild houses themselves are mostly private or restaurants and cannot be visited as a museum, but some house a restaurant or café you can go into.

To see the quays from the water, take a boat tour: several companies leave from here all year round, for a trip of about forty-five minutes through the old town. Do come back in the evening too, when the façades are lit.

name: St Michael’s Bridge
blurb: Built at the start of the 20th century, just before the 1913 World Fair. Look east to see Ghent’s three towers in a row: St Nicholas’, the Belfry and St Bavo’s. Behind you stands St Michael’s Church, whose tower was never finished.
text: St Michael’s Bridge is not a sight to look at so much as one to look from. From this stone arch over the Leie you get the finest view in Ghent. Look east and you see the city’s three towers in a neat row: first St Nicholas’ Church, then the Belfry with its dragon and behind it the tower of St Bavo’s Cathedral. Photographers and painters have stood here for more than a century.

Turn around and there is much more. Look north down the water, with the Graslei on the right and the Korenlei on the left, their guild houses mirrored in the Leie. In the distance the towers of the Gravensteen rise above the roofs. On the west side of the bridge stands St Michael’s Church, with its strikingly flat-topped tower, and on the east side the large neo-Gothic building of the old Post Office, now a hotel and shops.

The bridge itself is lovely in its simplicity: one broad arch in natural stone, with elegant lanterns and balustrades. In the evening, when the towers and the façades along the quays are lit, it is at its most romantic. No wonder it is called the romantic heart of Ghent, and that so many wedding photos are taken here.
history: There has been a bridge here since the Middle Ages, linking the old centre around the Korenmarkt with the quarter around St Michael’s Church across the Leie. It was a busy crossing, with the port on the Graslei and Korenlei right next to it.

The bridge you see now was built in the first years of the 20th century, in the run-up to the 1913 World’s Fair. Ghent wanted to show itself to the world as a medieval jewel, and the Graslei, the Gravensteen and the Belfry were all worked on in those years. The new bridge had to fit that picture, and be wide enough for modern traffic, trams included.

St Michael’s Church beside it is much older. Building of this Gothic church began in 1440 but dragged on for centuries through lack of money and the wars of religion. The tower was meant to be one of the tallest in the Low Countries but was never finished: hence its flat top. Inside hangs, among other things, a Crucifixion by Anthony van Dyck. The Post Office opposite was built between 1898 and 1909 in a rich mix of neo-Gothic and neo-Renaissance and, after a thorough conversion, found new life as a hotel and shopping centre.

visit: The bridge is always open to everyone and is on the Korenmarkt, a few steps from the Graslei. Come at sunrise for the calm, or at sunset and after, when the lights come on. It is the perfect starting point for a walk along the quays.

You can usually walk into St Michael’s Church for free, though its opening hours are shorter than the cathedral’s and often only in the tourist season. Mind the trams and cyclists crossing the bridge when you stop for a photo.

name: St Nicholas’ Church
blurb: The merchants’ church, from the 13th century, in blue-grey Tournai stone: Scheldt Gothic. Its tower sits right on the middle of the roof and doubled as a lookout, long before the Belfry stood. Today it also hosts concerts and exhibitions.
text: St Nicholas’ Church is the first of Ghent’s three towers you see coming from St Michael’s Bridge, and perhaps the most beautiful. It is built in Scheldt Gothic, a style found only in this region: plain, powerful Gothic in blue-grey stone from Tournai, shipped to Ghent down the Scheldt. Look at the corner turrets on the gables and at the great crossing tower, which does not stand at the front as on most churches but in the middle of the roof, above where nave and transept meet.

Inside, the church is surprisingly light and lofty. Its windows let plenty of daylight onto the pale stone, and you can see how the Gothic builders carried the weight of the roof with pillars and arches. There is a large Baroque high altar, and the impressive organ is the work of French organ builder Aristide Cavaillé-Coll, who also made the organs of Notre-Dame and Saint-Sulpice in Paris.
The church is still used for services, but also for concerts, exhibitions and events. Precisely because it stands on the bustling Korenmarkt, it is a good place to take a quiet moment.
history: St Nicholas’ is the merchants’ church. It stands on the Korenmarkt, where grain and other goods were traded in the Middle Ages, and was paid for by the city’s rich traders and guilds. St Nicholas is no coincidence: he is the patron saint of merchants and boatmen, among others. A Romanesque church stood here first; early in the 13th century work began on the Gothic church you see today.

The crossing tower long served as the city’s lookout. Watchmen kept an eye on the surroundings from it, and its bells called the townspeople together. When the Belfry was finished in the 14th century, it took over that role. Over the centuries the church was hit by fires, by the iconoclastic fury and by the French revolutionaries, who used it as a stable for a while.

From the 18th century on, little houses and shops grew up against its outer walls, until the church almost vanished behind a row of fronts. These were only cleared away in the 20th century. By then the church was in such a state that it had to close for a time. In the 1960s a long restoration began, which took decades and gave the church back the blue-grey beauty you see today.
dates: Building of the Gothic church begins.

visit: The church stands on the Korenmarkt, between St Michael’s Bridge and the Belfry, and is free to visit. It is usually open every day, on Mondays often only from midday, and during services and events part of it may be closed off. A visit takes about twenty minutes.
Keep an eye on what’s on: organ recitals and other concerts are held here regularly, and that is when you hear the Cavaillé-Coll organ at its best.

name: City Hall
blurb: A city hall in two styles: ornate late Gothic on the Hoogpoort, sober Renaissance on the Botermarkt. Running out of money and the wars of religion kept halting the building work. The Pacification of Ghent, a peace between the Low Countries’ provinces, was signed here in 1576.
text: Ghent’s Town Hall is really two buildings in one, as you see at once when you walk around it. On the Hoogpoort stands an exuberant late-Gothic front, full of stone lacework, pinnacles, niches and little balconies: it looks like a stone jewel box. Turn the corner onto the Botermarkt and you face a sober, stately Renaissance front with columns on three storeys, inspired by classical antiquity. The two styles don’t clash; together they tell the story of a city that spent a century building its town hall.

Inside are rooms from different centuries. The Pacification Hall, where the Pacification of Ghent was signed in 1576, has a floor with a maze pattern. The council meets and receptions are held in the Throne Room and the Arsenal Hall, and in the old Collation Hall and the Gothic chapel you see how the city’s rulers once presented themselves. The Town Hall is also where people in Ghent get married: every week couples step out here under the eyes of tourists.
The Town Hall is still the heart of Ghent’s government. The mayor and aldermen work here, and from the balcony on the Botermarkt champions and revellers are cheered.
history: In the Middle Ages the aldermen’s houses stood here, the buildings of the two benches of aldermen who ran the city. By the early 16th century Ghent was so rich and proud that it wanted a town hall to outshine every other in the Low Countries. In 1518 the master builders Rombout Keldermans and Domien de Waghemakere, who also worked in Antwerp and Mechelen, began the late-Gothic wing on the Hoogpoort.

Building soon stalled. In 1539 Ghent rose up against Charles V, lost its privileges and much of its money, and work stopped. Only in the late 16th and early 17th centuries did it go on, now in the new Renaissance style, with the front on the Botermarkt. The wars of religion and lack of money meant the Gothic wing was never finished to the original plan; part of it was only completed in the 19th century.

On 8 November 1576 the Pacification of Ghent was signed in the Town Hall. At a time of war between the Spanish king and the rebellious Netherlands, the provinces agreed to drive out the Spanish troops together and to tolerate each other despite their different faiths. It was a short-lived peace, but an important moment in the history of the Low Countries.

visit: The Town Hall is on the corner of the Hoogpoort and the Botermarkt, between the Belfry and the Vrijdagmarkt. You can’t just walk in: it is a working town hall. You see the inside on a guided tour, held at set times and often booked through Visit Gent. The outside you can of course look at any time, and it is well worth it.
Do walk all the way round the building to see both fronts, and on a Saturday see whether there is a wedding going on.

name: Vrijdagmarkt
blurb: The square of markets, feasts and uprisings, where the Counts of Flanders were sworn in. In the middle Jacob van Artevelde, the brewer who led Ghent in 1338, points the way. Across the square stands Ons Huis, the big home of the socialist workers’ movement.
text: The Vrijdagmarkt is one of the largest and oldest squares in Ghent, and for centuries it was the political heart of the city. It is a broad, open square, ringed by houses with stepped gables, Baroque fronts and big 19th-century buildings, with café terraces all around. In the middle stands the bronze statue of Jacob van Artevelde, pointing west with his arm outstretched: towards England, the country with which he made a crucial deal.

There is a lot to discover around the square. The large Ons Huis (Our House), with its rich, colourful front full of inscriptions, was the headquarters of the socialist labour movement. On the corner stands the Toreken, the tanners’ guild house with its slender tower, now a poetry centre. And at the Dulle Griet café you drink beer from a ‘Max’, a glass of more than a litre, for which you have to hand over one of your shoes as a deposit; it is then hoisted in a basket to the ceiling.

Right next to the square, on the Grootkanonplein, is the Dulle Griet (Mad Meg), a huge red wrought-iron cannon from the 15th century, one of the largest medieval cannons to survive. It was never really used in battle, but it is a much-loved symbol of the city.
history: The name says it all: a market has been held here every Friday (vrijdag) since the Middle Ages. But the Vrijdagmarkt was much more than a market square. This is where the Counts of Flanders were sworn in on their ceremonial entry and promised to respect the city’s rights. Here the guilds gathered, tournaments and feasts were held, and executions too.

In the 14th century Ghent was caught in the Hundred Years’ War between France and England. Ghent lived from cloth-making and needed English wool. In 1338 the wealthy merchant Jacob van Artevelde took charge of the city and kept Flanders neutral, so the wool kept coming. His power did not last: in 1345 he was murdered in a popular uprising. That same year the square saw ‘Evil Monday’, a bloody street battle between the weavers and the fullers that left hundreds dead.

In the 19th century, as Ghent became an industrial city, the Vrijdagmarkt became the square of the labour movement. Around 1900 the Vooruit cooperative built Ons Huis here, with shops, a café and meeting halls for the workers. The statue of Van Artevelde, by Pieter De Vigne, arrived in 1863. Today the square is above all a friendly place of terraces, with an underground car park beneath it.

visit: The Vrijdagmarkt is a public square, always open to all, five minutes’ walk from the Gravensteen and the Town Hall. There is still a market on Friday mornings, and often on Saturdays too. Around the square you can eat and drink on plenty of terraces.
Combine your visit with a walk to the Great Butchers’ Hall and the Patershol, or across the bridge to the Dulle Griet cannon and the Kraanlei.

name: Groot Vleeshuis
blurb: The butchers’ covered meat hall, built from 1406 to 1419. Hams still hang drying under its impressive wooden roof. Today you can buy and taste East Flemish regional produce here.
text: The Great Butchers’ Hall is a long, low hall of grey natural stone on the Leie, with stepped gables at both ends and a row of small dormers. From outside it looks modest, but step inside and you look straight up: the timber roof, an ingenious web of 15th-century oak beams, spans the whole hall without a single pillar in the middle. It is one of the finest medieval timber structures in the country.

Under those beams dozens of Ghent hams still hang drying, as the butchers did centuries ago. Today the hall is a showcase for East Flemish regional produce. You can taste and buy: Ghent mustard, neuzekes (Ghent’s purple cone-shaped sweets), local cheeses, jenever, beer and of course ham. There is also a café where you can eat a regional dish.

Outside, look at the little houses leaning against the wall on the Groentenmarkt: the penshuisjes (tripe houses). That is where the cheaper offal and tripe were sold, which were not allowed in the hall itself. At the back of the hall is a small chapel where the butchers had their mass.
history: In the Middle Ages meat could not just be sold anywhere in Ghent. The butchers’ guild had the monopoly, and all fresh meat had to be offered in this one covered hall, under the city’s supervision. That way the city could check that the meat was fresh and the right taxes were paid. The Great Butchers’ Hall was built between 1406 and 1419, on the site of an older meat hall.

The butchers’ guild was one of the richest and most powerful in the city, and membership passed from father to son. For centuries the people of Ghent came here to buy their meat. The tripe houses were later built against the wall for selling offal and sausages, which the butchers did not want inside the hall.

When the guilds disappeared at the end of the 18th century, the hall lost its purpose. It was used as a warehouse, among other things, and fell into disrepair. After a thorough restoration it gained a new role at the start of the 21st century as a meeting place for good East Flemish food, and so the hams hang there again as they used to.

21st century
After restoration: a centre for East Flemish produce.
visit: The Great Butchers’ Hall is on the Groentenmarkt, between the Korenmarkt and the Gravensteen, on the Leie. It is free to visit during the opening hours of the shop and café, usually Tuesday to Sunday. Pop in quickly to look at the roof, or take your time to taste and have lunch.
It is the ideal place to take an edible souvenir of Ghent home. From across the Leie you get the best view of the hall’s long front.

name: Graffiti Street
blurb: The Werregarenstraatje: since the 1990s anyone may spray paint here, legally. The walls get a fresh layer of paint almost every week, so no two visits look the same.
text: The Werregarenstraatje is a narrow lane between the Hoogpoort and the Onderstraat, a few steps from the Town Hall and the Vrijdagmarkt. It is only short, but every square centimetre of its walls, doors, gutters and sometimes even the ground is covered in graffiti. It is Belgium’s best-known legal graffiti street, and an open-air gallery that never stays the same.

You find all sorts here: colourful, technically brilliant ‘pieces’ by experienced graffiti artists, quick tags, stencils, stickers, political messages, funny little figures and beginners’ first attempts. Because anyone may spray here, everything is painted over all the time. A work you photograph today may be gone tomorrow. On some walls the layers of paint are by now centimetres thick.

The lane is above all a place to look around, take photos and stop for a moment by the artists you often see at work. It is also an interesting contrast with the medieval buildings right next to it: old and new Ghent a few metres apart.
history: The name refers to ‘werregaren’, a kind of yarn or thread that was worked in this area in the Middle Ages: a reminder of the days when Ghent lived from textiles. For a long time it was an ordinary, rather forgotten back street.

In the 1990s the city decided to open the lane to graffiti, as a place where young people and artists could go about it legally. The idea was that there would be less illegal graffiti on historic buildings if there was a place where it was allowed. The lane became a byword in the graffiti world and now draws many tourists too.

Ghent now has more places where graffiti is legal, and the city is known for its street art. Every year new murals appear around town, sometimes by internationally known artists. The Werregarenstraatje remains where that story began.
dates: Middle Ages
The street is named after werregaren yarn.
The city opens the lane to legal graffiti.
Today
A new layer of paint every week.
visit: The Werregarenstraatje is always open and free. You reach it from the Hoogpoort, close to the Town Hall, or from the Onderstraat on the Vrijdagmarkt side. A quick visit takes only a few minutes, but if you look closely you will stay longer.
Want to spray yourself? You may, as long as you respect the neighbours: don’t spray on windows, house doors or parked bikes, and take your empty cans with you.

name: Kouter
blurb: Ghent’s smartest square, once a field and a place for parades and archers’ feasts. There has been a flower market here every Sunday since the 18th century, with a brass band in the bandstand. The blue kiosk serves a drink to go with it.
text: The Kouter is Ghent’s grand, elegant square, on the south side of the old centre, a few minutes from the Veldstraat. It is broad and bright, ringed by stately 18th- and 19th-century mansions, banks and the Handelsbeurs concert hall. In the middle stands a graceful bandstand, and at the edge the well-known blue kiosk, where you can get a drink and a bite.

Every Sunday morning the Kouter becomes a sea of flowers and plants: the flower market is a Ghent tradition centuries old. Locals come to buy their bouquet or houseplant, drink a glass of cava or white wine with oysters at the kiosk, and listen to the band playing in the bandstand. It is one of the cosiest moments of the Ghent week.
On weekdays the Kouter is quieter, a place to cross on the way to Opera Ghent just behind the square, or to enjoy the sun on a bench for a moment.
history: A ‘kouter’ is an old Flemish word for open, shared farmland. In the early Middle Ages this square was indeed fields just outside the city. When Ghent grew and the area came to lie within the walls, the big open space remained.

In the late Middle Ages the Kouter became the square for parades, musters, tournaments and the festivities of the archers’ guilds, who practised here with their crossbows and longbows. Public ceremonies were held here too. In the 18th century it became the square of Ghent’s nobility and wealthy citizens, who had their mansions built around it.

The flower market began in the 18th century and has been there ever since. Ghent is a true city of flowers: the surrounding area is known for ornamental horticulture, with begonias, azaleas and more, and the Ghent Floralies have been one of the world’s largest flower shows since the 19th century. In the 19th century came the bandstand and, just behind the square, the Opera; with the Handelsbeurs concert hall they make the Kouter a cultural centre.
dates: Early Middle Ages
Farmland outside the city.
Late Middle Ages
Square for parades, tournaments and archers’ festivities.
18th century
The weekly flower market begins; noble mansions.
Opera Ghent just behind the square.
19th century
The bandstand.
visit: The Kouter is a public square and always open to all. The flower market is on Sunday mornings, roughly from 7 am to 1 pm, and it is at its liveliest between 10 and 12. It is an easy walk from the Korenmarkt along the Veldstraat, or take the tram, which stops close by.
Combine a visit with a stroll down the Veldstraat, Ghent’s main shopping street, or a performance at the Opera or the Handelsbeurs.

name: Vooruit
blurb: The party hall of the socialist co-operative Vooruit, opened in 1914: workers came here to dance, for theatre and concerts, and to eat in the café. Artists rescued it from decay in the 1980s. Today it is the arts centre VIERNULVIER.
text: Vooruit is a large, striking building on the Sint-Pietersnieuwstraat, with two little towers, a rich front mixing Art Nouveau and eclectic styles, and big windows that glow warmly in the evening. It was built as a festival hall for working people, and that still shows: inside there is a large ballroom with balconies, a theatre, smaller halls, stairwells with stained glass and, on the ground floor, a huge café.

Today it is one of the leading arts centres in Flanders, under the name VIERNULVIER. There are concerts, from rock and electronica to jazz and world music, theatre and dance, talks, debates, parties and festivals. The ground-floor café is open to everyone, ticket or not, and is a much-loved meeting place for students, artists and neighbours.

Being close to the university, Vooruit feels like the living room of student life in Ghent. On a terrace across the street, with a view of the lit-up front, you get a real sense of how lively this neighbourhood is.
history: Vooruit (Forward) was originally a socialist cooperative, founded in Ghent in 1880. It began as a cooperative bakery where workers together bought good, cheap bread; the profits went to set up other shops, a pharmacy, a health fund and cultural activities. The movement grew into a large organisation that shaped the lives of thousands of Ghent working families.

Between 1911 and 1914 the cooperative had this festival hall built, designed by architect Ferdinand Dierkens. It was meant to show working people that culture, fun and beauty were for them too, not just for the rich middle class. Balls, plays, concerts, congresses and meetings were held here, and the café was full every day.

After the Second World War the building lost its purpose; the halls fell into disrepair and there was even talk of demolition. In the early 1980s young artists and culture lovers took the initiative to bring Vooruit back to life as an arts centre. The building was listed and restored step by step. In 2021 the arts centre was renamed VIERNULVIER; the building itself is still called Vooruit.
dates: The socialist cooperative Vooruit is founded.
The festival hall is built, designed by Ferdinand Dierkens.
After 1945
Decline; the halls fall out of use.
A fresh start as an arts centre.
The arts centre is renamed VIERNULVIER.
visit: Vooruit is on the Sint-Pietersnieuwstraat, about ten minutes’ walk from the Korenmarkt, in the student quarter. The café is usually open every day, from late morning until late at night, and you can just walk in. For concerts and shows you buy a ticket; they often sell out fast.
Now and then there are guided tours of the building, which take you behind the scenes of its halls.

name: St Peter’s Abbey
blurb: The abbey on the Blandijnberg hill was founded in the 7th century, by Saint Amand as the story goes, and grew into one of the richest in Flanders. The baroque church with its dome (1629-1720) is by Pieter Huyssens. The French dissolved the abbey in 1796; today it is an exhibition hall, with an abbey garden of vines and ruins behind its walls.
text: St Peter’s Abbey stands on the Blandijnberg, the highest point of the old city, on the large Sint-Pietersplein. What you see first is the Baroque church of Our Lady of St Peter, with its stately front and great dome, which rises above the roofs from afar. Beside the church lie the former abbey buildings, around a cloister, with a refectory, a chapter house and cellars that are in places centuries old.

Today the abbey buildings are an exhibition hall, holding major shows on art, history and the world today. Behind the walls lies a hidden gem: the abbey garden. There you find a vegetable garden, fruit trees, a herb garden, the ruins of older abbey buildings and even a vineyard on the slope, a reminder of the monks who made wine here for centuries. It is one of the quietest spots in the city.
The Sint-Pietersplein in front is one of the largest squares in Ghent. It is used for funfairs, circuses, events and markets, and lies close to the university quarter and Citadelpark.
history: According to tradition, St Amand founded a monastery here in the 7th century, on the Blandijnberg overlooking the meeting of the Leie and the Scheldt. The abbey grew into one of the richest and most powerful in Flanders, with vast estates and a great library. For a long time it was the great rival of St Bavo’s Abbey on the other side of the city.

In the 9th century the abbey was sacked by the Vikings, but it was rebuilt. Counts of Flanders were buried here, and the abbey played a large part in the life of the city. It was badly hit by the iconoclastic fury of 1566. Afterwards it was rebuilt, and between 1629 and 1720 the present Baroque church rose, designed by the Jesuit architect Pieter Huyssens.

In 1796 the French revolutionaries abolished the abbey, as they did all monasteries. The monks had to leave and the property was sold. The buildings were later used as barracks, among other things. Only in the 20th century did they get a new role as a cultural centre and exhibition space. The abbey garden was restored and is now a public green heart in the city.
dates: 7th century
Founded, by tradition, by St Amand.
9th century
Sacked by the Vikings.
Badly hit by the iconoclastic fury.
The Baroque church is built, after Pieter Huyssens.
The French abolish the abbey.
20th century
New life as an exhibition space and art hall.
visit: The abbey is on the Sint-Pietersplein, about fifteen minutes’ walk from the centre, or by tram to nearby. The abbey garden is usually free to enter during the day, with shorter hours in winter. For the exhibitions in the art hall you buy a ticket. The church is regularly open to visitors.
Combine a visit with a walk to Citadelpark, S.M.A.K. or the Museum of Fine Arts, all within walking distance.

name: Gent Zuid
blurb: Until 1928 the Zuidstation, Ghent’s first railway station, stood here. Today it is De Lijn’s hub: most city buses start and end here, and the trams pass on their way to the centre and Sint-Pieters.
text: ‘Zuid’ (South), as Ghent people simply call it, is the area around the Woodrow Wilsonplein and the Frère-Orbanlaan, just south-east of the old centre. It isn’t a classic sight, but as a visitor you will almost certainly pass through it: it is Ghent’s main public transport hub. Most of De Lijn’s city buses meet here, and the trams pass by on their way to the centre, Gent-Sint-Pieters station and the edge of town.

Around the square are the Zuid shopping centre, offices, flats and the large former library building. Close by is the King Albert Park, a green strip of trees and lawns where the railway once ran, with a monument to King Albert I. It is a lively, rather busy area, where you can see how modern Ghent works and lives.
For exploring the city, Zuid is a handy starting point: from here it is a ten-minute walk to the Kouter and the Korenmarkt, and a few minutes by tram to the station or the centre.
history: In 1837 Ghent got its first station, the South Station, on the site of today’s square. It was a splendid building with a great hall, and one of the first railway stations in the country: Belgium was a railway pioneer on the European mainland. Around the station grew a new, smart neighbourhood of broad avenues and mansions.

Early in the 20th century Gent-Sint-Pieters station was built, in the run-up to the 1913 World’s Fair. It gradually took over the South Station’s role, and the old station closed in 1928. The building was then torn down, and the tracks made way for the King Albert Park and the Woodrow Wilsonplein, named after the American president of the First World War.

In the second half of the 20th century Zuid became the hub of the city buses, and the shopping centre and the city library arrived. The library moved in 2017 to De Krook, on the Scheldt. Today there is thinking about the area’s future, to make it greener and more pleasant for those who live in it and pass through.
dates: The South Station opens, Ghent’s first.
The new Gent-Sint-Pieters station.
The South Station closes and is pulled down.
Late 20th century
Bus hub, shopping centre and library.
The library moves to De Krook.
visit: Zuid is always open to all. Most city buses stop here, and the trams too. For timetables and tickets, the De Lijn website or app is the place to look.
If you want something to eat or drink, there are plenty of places in and around the shopping centre. For a break, head into the King Albert Park.

name: Blaarmeersen
blurb: Ghent’s sports and leisure park, by the Watersportbaan. On hot days the beach on the swimming lake is packed, and joggers run their laps round the 2.3 km rowing course. There is also a campsite, an athletics track and beach volleyball.
text: The Blaarmeersen is Ghent’s large sports and leisure park, on the west side of the city, a quarter of an hour by bike from the centre. It is a green oasis of woods, lawns and water, around a big swimming lake with a sandy beach. On hot summer days it feels like the seaside: hundreds of Ghent people lie on the beach, swim, play beach volleyball or picnic on the grass.

Along the park runs the Watersportbaan, a dead-straight rowing course more than two kilometres long. Rowers and kayakers train there, and it is a favourite running route: the loop round the water is the regular circuit of many Ghent joggers. There is also an athletics track, tennis courts, a skate park, mini golf, playgrounds, a climbing wall, footpaths and cycle paths, and a campsite.
The park borders a nature reserve with reed beds and ponds, where you can spot birds. So the Blaarmeersen is at once a sports park, a city beach and a bit of nature, all within the city limits.
history: ‘Meersen’ are wet, low-lying meadows along a river, and that is what this area was for centuries: marshy grassland along the Leie, often under water in winter. The name Blaarmeersen recalls that old landscape.

In the 1950s the Watersportbaan was dug here, a long, straight rowing course for international races. Ghent hosted major rowing championships on it, and the course became a byword in the rowing world. The earth that was dug out was used to raise the land beside it.

In the decades that followed the Blaarmeersen grew into a big leisure park for the whole city, with the swimming lake, the beach, sports grounds and the campsite. For many people in Ghent without a garden or a trip to the sea, it is the place to cool off in summer, and the place for sport all year round.
dates: For centuries
Wet meadows along the Leie.
The Watersportbaan is dug.
Today
Beach, sport, camping and nature a quarter of an hour from the centre.
visit: The park is open to all. The beach and swimming lake are open in the summer months, with lifeguards, for a small entrance fee. It is easy to get there by bike, along the Leie or the Watersportbaan, or by bus. The campsite and sports facilities have their own opening hours and bookings.
On a summer’s day, bring your swimming things and a picnic, and come early if you can: on the hottest days it gets busy.

name: Mammelokker
blurb: Look above the door of this little house against the Cloth Hall: a young woman giving an old man her breast. It is the Roman legend of Pero, who nursed her father Cimon when he was left to starve in prison. When it came out, he was set free. The warders of the town prison, which was in the Cloth Hall’s cellars from 1742 to 1902, lived here. Mammelokker is Ghent dialect for breast-sucker. The relief dates from 1741, recarved by Jan Anteunis in 1962.
text: The Mammelokker is the little house against the foot of the Cloth Hall, where the warders of the town prison lived: from 1742 to 1902 the prison was in the Cloth Hall’s cellars. Over its door a stone relief from 1741, recarved by Jan Anteunis in 1962, shows a young woman feeding an old man at her breast.

It is the Roman legend of Pero, who nursed her father Cimon when he was left to starve in prison; when it came out, he was set free. Ghent named the house after it: mammelokker is Ghent dialect for breast-sucker.

name: Karel Sabbeberg
blurb: Ghent’s only mountain, some 30 metres high, and man-made. Until 2003 Ghent skied here on brush mats. In 2019 it was named after the ultrarunner Karel Sabbe, who ran up and down it thousands of times in training. Since 2009 a lookout tower on top looks out over the city.
text: Ghent’s only mountain is some 30 metres high and man-made, in the Blaarmeersen park. Until 2003 Ghent skied down it on brush mats. In 2019 it was named after the ultrarunner Karel Sabbe, who ran up and down it thousands of times in training.

Since 2009 a wooden lookout tower stands on top, from which you see over the lakes and the woods of the park to the towers of the old town. In the game it hides a secret for whoever climbs all the way up.

name: Cuberdons
blurb: Purple cone-shaped sweets with a runny raspberry heart, sold from little carts on the Groentenmarkt.
text: A cuberdon, or neuzeke (“little nose”) in Ghent, is a cone of gum arabic with a hard sugary crust and a soft, syrupy inside that tastes of raspberry. Because the crust dries out and the inside crystallises within a few weeks, they never really travelled, and they stayed a Belgian, and above all a Ghent, treat.

On the Groentenmarkt, right by the Groot Vleeshuis, two sellers have stood facing each other with their carts for years, and their feud over who sells the real neuzekes has become a local legend. In the game you ride past them.

name: The trams
blurb: De Lijn’s white and yellow trams, ringing their bells through the narrow streets of the old town.
text: Ghent has run trams since the 19th century, first pulled by horses, and it is one of the few Belgian cities that kept them. Today De Lijn’s lines 1, 2 and 4 cross the city, squeezing through the old centre along the Korenmarkt and the Kortrijksesteenweg, where they share the cobbles with cyclists and people on foot.
In the game the trams run on their real lines, stop at their real stops and ring their bells at whoever is in the way. Mind the rails on a bike: wheels and tram tracks do not get on.

name: Gentse Feesten
blurb: Ten days every July when the whole old town becomes one of the largest street festivals in Europe.
text: The Gentse Feesten began in 1843 as a way to give the city’s workers a holiday of their own, and grew into a ten-day festival in the middle of July. Every square of the old town gets a stage, from the Vrijdagmarkt to the Sint-Baafsplein, with music, street theatre and puppet shows, much of it free.
More than a million visitors come over those ten days. The festival ends on the “Dag van de Lege Portemonnee”, the day of the empty wallet, when the city sleeps it off.

name: The cycling city
blurb: Since 2017 cars can no longer drive straight across the centre, and bikes have taken over the streets.
text: In 2017 Ghent split its centre into sections that cars can only reach from the ring road, not from one another. Through traffic disappeared almost overnight, and the number of cyclists shot up. Many streets became fietsstraten, bicycle streets, where cars are guests and may not overtake a bike.
That is why the game starts you on a bike: it is how most people in Ghent get about, past the three towers and along the Leie.
